transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. I'm Dr. Smith. To start, can you tell me what's been bothering you or what brings you in today?
I’ve been worrying a lot, and once it gets started I can’t seem to switch it off. Even if I make a list, check the dates, and know I’ve done what I can, my mind just keeps going over it.
How long have you been experiencing this ongoing worry—has it been present most days for six months or more, or did it start more recently after a specific event?
It’s been about seven months now. It started shortly after my friend died, when I was trying to keep our projects moving.

Is your worry mainly centered on things related to your friend's death and the projects you're managing, or do you find yourself worrying about many different areas of your life—like health, finances, family, work—even things unrelated to that loss?

It’s not just about my friend or the projects. My mind jumps around—the exhibition schedule, my daughter’s travel plans, whether the gutters need fixing. Little things start to feel like they could turn into something much bigger.
Along with all this worrying, have you noticed physical symptoms like feeling restless or on edge, muscle tension, or unusual fatigue?
Yes. I often feel wound up even sitting in my own living room. I’ll tap my fingers during phone calls, or get up and straighten something because sitting still makes me feel jumpy.
Have you noticed any changes in your sleep, such as trouble falling asleep, staying asleep, or feeling that your sleep isn't restful, since this worrying began?
I’m not really sure I’ve noticed a change in my sleep.
Have you noticed any trouble concentrating or your mind going blank because of the worrying?
I’m not sure. I haven’t really noticed my mind going blank or anything like that.
Have you noticed feeling more irritable or on edge with others since this worrying started?
I do feel pretty on edge. Even at home, I’m often wound up—tapping my fingers on the phone or getting up to straighten things because I can’t seem to sit quietly.

Associated symptoms include motor restlessness/being 'on edge' and irritability, along with muscle tension (fidgeting, needing to move). These symptoms meet criteria for Generalized Anxiety Disorder.
